newsitem.title: USA: GM workers in Indiana ratify pact to end strike.
newsitem.headline: GM workers in Indiana ratify pact to end strike.

text.p: Workers at General Motors Corp's truck plant in Fort Wayne, Ind., voted to ratify a new local labor agreement late Thursday night that ends a nearly two week strike over staffing levels.
Members of United Auto Workers Local 2209 approved the deal by an 85 percent margin. It calls for GM to add 276 workers to the plant's payroll.

Production of Chevrolet C/K and GMC Sierra full-size pickup trucks at the plant is scheduled to resume on Tuesday. Like all of GM's U.S. factories, the plant is not scheduled to operate Friday or Monday because of the Easter holiday.

Local 2209's 2,700 members walked off the job on March 14 to pressure GM to reach a new local labor agreement at the plant. The deal, which also includes improvements in vacation and other benefits, fulfills the union's demands for more manpower to deal with an increasing workload prompted by strong demand for its trucks and by GM's moves to boost efficiency.

"The jobs issue was the nucleus of the problems in the plant," said Local 2209 President Joseph Burkhamer. "With the addition of these people, this is going to give us the ability to build the number one quality vehicle in the world."

Most of the new workers at the plant will likely be transferred in from other GM facilities that have excess employees, he said, adding that some temporary workers may be hired for short periods until transferees are located.

The walkout caused GM to lose production of about 10,000 of the popular pickup trucks, which Wall Street analysts estimate will reduce the automaker's first quarter earnings by as much as $50 million, or 7 cents a share.
Lehman Brothers analyst Joseph Phillippi, however, said he believes GM can make up most of the lost production during the second quarter.
The strike did not cause any shortages of the trucks in dealer showrooms because GM builds the same models at three other plants, in Pontiac and Flint, Mich., and Oshawa, Ontario.

GM has faced disputes over jobs at nearly all of its U.S. plants this year as it slowly grinds ahead with local UAW negotiations. The automaker is experiencing record rates of retirements and is aiming to improve its profitability in part by limiting the amount of new workers it hires to replace them.
On Wednesday, UAW Local 1999 in Oklahoma City notified GM that it would strike on April 4 if no local pact was reached by then, and the main sticking point remains jobs.
A strike in Oklahoma would largely cut off supplies of GM's critical new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass mid-size cars just as they are starting to appear in national advertising campaigns.

But Phillippi noted that if GM hires significant numbers of new workers at plants where it will build new products, it will lose some of the planned efficiency gains that it desperately needs to become competitive with rivals Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp.

The Fort Wayne plant, for example, next year will launch production of a new-generation full-size truck that will require 30 percent fewer labor hours to produce -- a situation that could leave GM with excess workers at the facility.

In its national agreement with the UAW, GM agreed to maintain employment at a level equal to 95 percent of its current hourly workforce. The pact allows the automaker to shed some of its 215,000 workers when it installs new technology. This typically occurs with a new car or truck model goes into production. However, hiring committments at individual plants like Fort Wayne could prevent GM from taking advantage of that provision.
